episodes.178209: An isolated supercell produced large hail and damaging winds in Cullman County during the early morning hours.
episodes.178256: On the evening of April 28, a line of strong thunderstorms developed ahead of an advancing cold front. This line of storm produced many instances of wind damage as well as some hail across SE TX, mainly to the north of the I-10 corridor.
episodes.178318: Warming temperatures into the 60s and 70s caused rock slides to occur.
episodes.178346: A weak low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley with a few storms producing hail.
episodes.178365: Strong thunderstorms produced severe hail, a funnel cloud, and severe wind gusts in Brevard County. A funnel cloud was also reported in Seminole County.
episodes.178385: A squall line associated with a MCS moving across the Eastern Gulf of Mexico produced a severe wind gust in Hernando County and wind damage in Sumter County, along with numerous 50+ mph sub-severe wind gusts across the Tampa Bay area after pushing ashore across the Florida west coast.
episodes.178400: A squall line associated with a MCS moving across the Eastern Gulf of Mexico produced gusty marine winds across all Florida west coast waters as it moved ashore, with a few severe gusts reported across the Tampa Bay Area and neighboring waters.
episodes.178477: A weak trough near the Leeward islands was maintaining a weak steering flow over the local islands. Instability aloft was increasing as mid level temperatures cool down. The combination of these factors, along with strong diurnal heating and enough moisture in the lower levels resulted in very strong showers and isolated thunderstorms over the area. Several reports of mudslides and flooding were received.
episodes.178486: An area of low pressure resulted in widespread two to four inches of rain. This resulted in a couple of road closures due to high water and small streams overflowing their banks.
episodes.178527: Strong to severe storms produced wind gusts along the Brevard and Volusia County Coasts.
episodes.178528: A thunderstorm pushing offshore from the Indian River County coast produced a strong wind gust.
episodes.178574: A couple thunderstorms turned severe during the very early morning hours of April 28, 2023. The strongest of these thunderstorms was near Columbia where one inch hail was reported. The most significant damage, however, was from lightning. Near Cookeville, a lightning strike severely damaged an apartment building while another home in Williamson County was also damaged from lightning.
episodes.178665: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed and spread northeast along a cold front that bisected Northeast Texas, ahead of an upper trough that moved into the Southern Plains during the afternoon of April 28th. The air mass aloft remained quite cold and unstable ahead of the trough, with large scale forcing enough for the development of isolated severe thunderstorms that spread into the western sections of East Texas during the late afternoon hours. One particular severe thunderstorm moved across Western Wood County, where quarter size hail fell just north of Alba along Lake Fork.
episodes.178729: A retreating area of high pressure over Virginia, and a northward advancing warm front moving into Virginia, set the stage for an unstable atmosphere prone for rotation over the Piedmont and Foothill region of North Carolina. By the afternoon hours, showers and storms starting forming, with a couple of these storms reached severe levels with hail and damaging winds. A shortly lived EF0 tornado occurred near Elkin in Surry County.
episodes.179097: A strong spring storm system moved through the area with ample instability and shear for severe weather. Numerous reports of severe weather were received across the tri-state area.  Two tornadoes occurred across southwest Georgia, and seven tornadoes occurred across the eastern Florida panhandle and big bend.  An EF2 tornado produced significant damage in the town of Hosford, FL.
episodes.179250: A round of afternoon thunderstorms blossomed in West Virginia on April 28th as a weak surface low was centered over the state. Instability was just enough to allow a few storms to reach strong thresholds. As storms passed through Madison, gusty winds blew down a tree and blocked both lanes of Pond Fork Road.
episodes.179269: Rapid snowmelt from a few day period of well above normal temperatures focused on the 11-13th of April resulted in moderate to locally major flooding through much of the James River Basin. Some areas north of I-90 lost between 2 to 5 inches of snow water equivalent (SWE) from the first to second week of April, but antecedent drought conditions resulted in only a percentage of this water actually making it into the river system.
episodes.179279: A frontal boundary and shortwave impulses aloft provided a source of lift, combined with instability, triggered offshore showers and thunderstorms the morning of April 28th.
episodes.179330: A pre-frontal through over a moist and unstable airmass formed across NE FL during the afternoon and evening which triggered scattered strong to severe storms as mesoscale boundaries collided. A second round of strong to severe storms impacted the area during the evening as a remnant MCS moved west to east across the area.
episodes.179333: A pre-frontal through over a moist and unstable airmass formed across NE FL during the afternoon and evening which triggered scattered strong to severe storms as mesoscale boundaries collided. A second round of strong to severe storms impacted the area during the evening as a remnant MCS moved west to east across the area.
episodes.179334: Southwest steering flow over a moist and unstable airmass produced a few strong to pulse severe storms during the afternoon.
episodes.179349: Scattered storms moved southeast across the Colorado state line into Northwest Kansas where they eventually formed a broken line of storms over Logan and Thomas counties. These storms produced severe wind gusts up to 62 mph, which was observed in Western Logan County. At times the winds also produced localized blowing dust, with visibility of less than one mile in Northeast Sherman County. These storms also produced small hail up to the size of peas in the city of Oakley, Kansas.
episodes.179604: Thunderstorms developed ahead of and along a cold front as it moved through South Central Texas. These storms produced large hail.
episodes.179624: While cool temperatures and rainy conditions were in place for the last several days of the month, there was one more round of strong to severe thunderstorms to move across the state on April 27th. A few storms produced hail from central into eastern Arkansas. A few brief funnel clouds also occurred across northeast Arkansas beneath an upper level storm system that rotated its way east of the area.
episodes.179744: A weak surface low moving northward across eastern Mississippi produced a few thunderstorms across west Alabama during the evening hours on Thursday, April 27th. Mid level lapse rates increased to near 7 degrees Celsius which allowed for the production of large hail in Tuscaloosa County.
episodes.179778: With the influence of a mid-level disturbance to the north, a surface frontal boundary sagged into South-Central Florida which put South Florida near a source of lift, combined with surface instability from diurnal heating. Additional shortwave impulses added to the convective activity and led to severe thunderstorm producing a tornado in Broward County on April 28th.
episodes.180027: A stationary front was draped across the Mid-South on April 27, 2023. A mid-level shortwave trough interacted with the front to produce scattered showers and thunderstorms. Steep mid-level lapse rates aided large hail development across the area.
episodes.180036: Widespread rainfall associated with a deep low pressure system and associated cold front occurred across the Piedmont region from late in the evening on the 27th through late morning on the 28th.  A Strong southerly flow of wind allowed precipitable water values during the early morning hours of the 28th to increase to around 1.3 inches across portions of the Piedmont, which is between the 75th and the 99th percentile for the end of April.  While this rainfall was mostly beneficial given the antecedent dryness, Ivy Creek in the western part of the City of Lynchburg was observed overflowing its banks due to 3.5 to nearly 4.5 inches of rainfall across nearly the entire basin.  Rainfall rates were generally below 0.5���/hr through most of the event, however these increased to as high as 2���/hr just ahead of the passage of a cold front on the morning of the 28th.  The flooded creek caused only minor damage to Peaks View Park, mainly in the form of cleanup of mud and small debris.
episodes.180054: Snowmelt flooding along the North Dakota Tributaries began in mid-April, with a few locations persisting into early May. These points are crests from the end of April.
episodes.180065: Another complex surface pattern unfolded on Friday April 28, comprising of a low pressure center, warm front, dryline, and Pacific cold front. All of these features contributed to the development of strong to severe thunderstorms as the next upper trough swept through the Plains. Storms developed shortly after noon, affected areas mainly south of I-20, and exited the region by 7 PM that evening. Large hail up to 3 inches was reported in Hamilton County, and an EF1 tornado occurred in Coryell County.
episodes.180965: Storms developed and produced large hail and damaging wind gusts.

A supercell tracked across Coryell County on the afternoon of April 28th producing an EF-1 tornado with maximum winds around 105 mph. The pattern of damage suggests this tornado may have been a multi-vortex tornado and evidence of very strong RFD wind damage was also found just south of the tornado track, further complicating the track location.||The tornado likely began near Bagget Mountain, tracked across CR 146, and did the most notable damage along CR 148. Several large trees along CR 148, in multiple locations, were damaged ranging from broken trunks to large trees uprooted. The property of a sporting range was damaged with the shooting range cover being blown across the street to the northeast. Two injuries occurred at this location, and one person was transported with a leg injury. The tornado generally followed CRs 148 and 147 on a southeast direction, continuing to damage trees and causing minor roof damage. The tornado crossed FM 116, just north of CR 145, causing  damage to trees and minor roof damage to a home east of the road.  The tornado then moved onto the property of Fort Hood. Access to this area is limited, but additional damage to trees and power poles was found along West Range Road, south of Henson Creek. The end of the tornado was estimated by radar over inaccessible areas of Fort Hood.||RFD winds were determined to be the cause of damage of a collapsed cell phone tower along West Range Road and a home on Longview Circle that lost part of its roof. The RFD winds could have been near 95 mph.

A tornado affected southern portions of Boynton Beach on the evening of April 28th. The first visible signs of tornadic damage were just west of I-95 and south of SW 23rd Ave in the form of several broken large tree branches and a royal palm tree partially stripped of its fronds. The tornado moved ENE continuing it's path as it crossed I-95, with reports of traffic stopping or slowing down as the circulation crossed the interstate. The tornado then moved through portions of the High Point community where about a half-dozen homes sustained minor roof uplift near the corners of the structures, awnings twisted or completely torn off and landing several houses away, and several large tree branches and trunks broken. The  final indication of tornadic damage was a downed small palm tree at Main Blvd, east of SW 3rd St, just south of the Boynton Beach Little League Park. The damage path was sporadic in spots, with large tree branches or trunks snapped right next to other trees and buildings with no visible signs of damage. Therefore, the tornado is rated as an EF-0 with estimated maximum winds near 80 mph. Most of the winds along the damage path were estimated in the 65-75 mph range. Damage amounts are estimated.
